prs.title: fix(finding): lock the finding before found_by on the v3 create and the v2/v3 updates
prs.body:
**Description**

The bulk-delete `found_by` deadlock fixed for `POST /api/v2/findings/` (#16950) is still there on the other writers that replace an existing finding's `found_by`: the v3 create (`services.create_finding`), the v3 update (`services.update_finding`, PATCH and PUT) and the v2 update (`FindingSerializer.update`, PATCH and PUT).

Each runs `found_by.set()` in its own transaction (`ATOMIC_REQUESTS` is off). `set()` deletes the rows that were not requested and inserts the requested ones, and both stay locked until COMMIT, where Postgres checks the new rows' deferred foreign key with `FOR KEY SHARE` on the finding. The chunked bulk delete (the excess-duplicate delete, a test or engagement delete) takes the same two locks the other way round: `lock_findings_for_delete` holds the finding `FOR UPDATE`, then `bulk_clear_finding_m2m` deletes its `found_by` rows. Each waits for the other and Postgres aborts one with `deadlock detected` (40P01).

This change sends those three writers through `set_found_by_locking_finding_first`, the helper the v2 create already uses, which locks the finding `FOR KEY SHARE` before writing `found_by`, the order the delete uses. The helper moves from `dojo/finding/api/serializer.py` to `dojo/finding/helper.py` (next to `lock_findings_for_delete`) so `dojo/finding/services.py` can use it without importing the API serializer; the serializer imports it from there, so its name in that module is unchanged.

`clear()` (a writer sent `found_by: []`) is left as it is. It only deletes rows, so its COMMIT checks no foreign key and never waits on the finding, and it was measured not to deadlock (below).

Measured on a Postgres-backed stack:

- **Reproduction.** Two connections. Connection A runs the writer as production runs it (autocommit, no request transaction) and pauses inside its `found_by` write; connection B runs the delete's order (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the finding, then `DELETE` of its `found_by` rows). 3 rounds per writer:

  | writer | before | after |
  |---|---|---|
  | v2 create (control, fixed by #16950) | 0/3 | 0/3 |
  | v3 create | 3/3 deadlocked | 0/3 |
  | v2 update, `set()` | 3/3 deadlocked | 0/3 |
  | v3 update, `set()` | 3/3 deadlocked | 0/3 |
  | v2 update, `clear()` | 0/3 | 0/3 |
  | v3 update, `clear()` | 0/3 | 0/3 |

  After the change every write returns 200/201 (or completes, for the services), and the delete waits for the writer instead of deadlocking.
- **Cost.** One extra query per `found_by` write: v2 update 47 to 48, v3 update 25 to 26, v3 create 39 to 40. The added statement is a primary-key index scan: 0.066 ms execution, 0.40 ms median round trip (p99 0.58 ms, n=1000) on the stack's table, and 0.042 ms execution, 0.28 ms median round trip (p99 0.50 ms) on a 2,000,000-row table of the same shape. Per-request medians before and after overlap: on the shared host the same unchanged code varied more between rounds (62 to 215 ms for the v3 update) than any before/after difference.

**Test results**

- `unittests/test_finding_create_found_by_lock_order.py`: new `TestFindingFoundByWritersLockOrder`, one test per writer (v3 create, v3 update, v2 PATCH). Each pins that the finding's `FOR KEY SHARE` lock comes before `set()`'s `dojo_finding_found_by` delete and insert, and that `found_by` ends up as requested. On `dev` all three fail (no lock before the write); with this change all 5 tests in the file pass. The `found_by`-write matcher now also finds a write that pghistory prefixes with its context inside a request.
- `unittests/api_v3` (finding writes, findings, findings query counts, query report, conflict, examples): pass.
- `unittests/test_dedupe_delete_commit_race`: the same tests fail with and without this change in the local container used here (environmental), identical failure set; CI runs the module in its own image.
- `ruff check` (pinned 0.16.10) passes on the whole tree.

**Documentation**

No user-visible change; no documentation needed.

prs.author: blakeaowens
prs.title: fix(migrations): wait for a 0307 index build to commit before judging it invalid
prs.body:
**Description**

`AddHistoryLookupIndexes` in migration `0307_event_history_lookup_indexes` waits while `pg_stat_progress_create_index` shows another backend building an index, then reads `pg_index.indisvalid` and drops and rebuilds the index when it is not valid. Postgres ends a concurrent build's progress row just before the build's last transaction commits, and that transaction is the one that sets `indisvalid`. In that window the wait sees no build, `indisvalid` still reads false, and `_add` runs `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on an index that was about to become valid: the index is built again from scratch, or the drop fails with `tuple concurrently updated`.

This is the same defect #16981 fixed in `0305_archive_batch_indexes`; 0307 carries its own copy of the wait.

**Fix:** `_build_in_progress` in 0307 now uses the same check as 0305. Besides the progress row, a build counts as in progress while the index's `pg_index` row has an uncommitted update: its `xmax` names a transaction that still holds the lock on its own id in `pg_locks` (every transaction holds that lock until it ends, and `pg_locks` is readable without extra privileges). The existing bounded wait loop then covers the window. Migration state is unchanged.

**Test results**

New test `HistoryLookupIndexBuildCommitTest.test_build_ending_is_waited_for_until_it_commits` in `unittests/test_auditlog_history_indexes.py`, modelled on the test in #16981. It holds a real `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` of `dojo_findingevt_test_hist` on `dojo_findingevent` in the commit window with no timing: a `ddl_command_end` event trigger waits on an advisory lock the test holds. The test checks that state directly (no progress row, `indisvalid` false), runs the operation, and releases the lock from the operation's first sleep. 0307 issues its drop through a raw cursor rather than the schema editor, so the test refuses any `DROP INDEX` through `connection.execute_wrapper` and fails fast instead of hanging. Creating an event trigger needs a superuser; the test skips otherwise.

Measured on PostgreSQL 18 (the compose image):

| | `0307` from `dev` | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| new test, as a superuser | failed: `dropped an index whose build had not committed yet: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS "dojo_findingevt_test_hist"` (from `_add`, line 113) | OK |
| `_build_in_progress` as a non-superuser, for an idle existing index and a missing one | | `False`, `False`, no error |
| cost of one `_build_in_progress` call (mean of 2000) | 0.35 ms, 1 query | 3.1 ms, 1 query |

The check runs once per index (34) and once per 5 s poll while waiting, so the added cost per migration run is about 0.1 s.

- The other tests in `unittests/test_auditlog_history_indexes.py`: unchanged results.
- `makemigrations dojo --check --dry-run`: No changes detected.
- `ruff check .` (0.16.10): All checks passed.

#16971 copies the old wait into further concurrent-index migrations; those copies need the same check and are not changed here.

**Documentation**

None needed: no user-facing change.

prs.author: dmpetrov
prs.title: Listing: write directly without UDF
prs.body:
Step 3 of 3 of phase 1 (redesign) in epic #2223; review the steps in order: #2220 → #2221 → #2222. It depends on #2221 and is based on its branch.

### What
- **Listing as a producer.** Listing no longer runs as a `gen` UDF over a 1-row seed dataset.
  8 child processes list key ranges and encode rows with `RowCodec`, and the parent inserts the stored rows directly into the reserved version table.
- **Order-independent digest in `content_hash`.** A 128-bit `blake2b` sum over rows (`listing-v1:{count}:{digest}`) is independent of child page order and reuses `content_hash` (unused on listings) so no SQLite/PostgreSQL schema migration is needed. An unchanged refresh drops its new version and restarts the TTL on the existing version.
- **Pre-scan reservation & publish.** Unlike `save()`, listing reserves its `CREATED` version before scanning (avoiding `tmp_*` tables, which `datachain gc` drops unconditionally) and refreshes `created_at` every 5 minutes during long scans.

### Deleted
- the listing seed dataset and gen UDF, `list_bucket`;
- `calc_fingerprint`, `_reuse_listing_if_unchanged`, the `save(listing=True)` branches;
- `write_listing`'s `file_type`, `settings` and `in_memory` arguments.

### Lines (excluding tests)
`+273/-206 (+67 total)` in `src/` (Phase 1 total across #2220–#2222: `+2246/-2274 (-28 total)`).

### Performance
Phase 2 → this PR. Same setup as #2220; real S3, 1.67M objects.

| operation | phase 2 | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| list_storage | 12.6 | 10.9 |
| read_storage, first listing | 35.0 | 14.7 |
| read_storage, unchanged refresh | 35.4 | 14.0 |

Stored listing rows are byte-identical to main.

### Behaviour changes
- `read_storage` and `ls` create no job and no seed dataset.
- The listing dataset's schema is always `File`.
- `DataChain.hash()` of chains over a listing changes; older listings refresh once.

### Studio
- The listing names Studio imports are unchanged.

prs.title: Fix annotation updates when the end time changes
prs.body:
## Description

Posting an annotation with a changed end time can return HTTP 500. The lookup includes end and omits belief_time, while the database uniqueness constraint includes belief_time and excludes end. Extending an existing EV label from 07:00 to 07:15 therefore attempts a conflicting insert.

Align the lookup with the database identity: content, start, belief time, source and type. When an annotation already exists, update its end time and reuse it. Preserve separate annotations for different belief times.

Regression tests cover extending an annotation, repeating the request and preserving distinct belief times. The failure and fix were also reproduced locally using v1.1.1’s annotation model on an isolated SQLite database; the full server test suite has not been run.

Found while working on the HEMS script, as I made annotations longer.

- [x] fix updating/extending existing annotaitons - align annotation lookup…so it plays well with its database uniqueness constraint

prs.author: Flix6x
prs.title: Fix dropping unchanged beliefs in the repeated hour of a clock change
prs.body:
## Description

Saving beliefs first drops those that are unchanged compared to what is stored (`_drop_unchanged_beliefs_compared_to_db`).
That comparison puts the stored beliefs, which come back from the database in UTC, and the new beliefs, which may be in local time, into one key column.

In the hour that an autumn clock change repeats (e.g. 02:00-03:00 in Europe/Amsterdam on 26 October 2025), a time in the second pass (`fold=1`, 02:15+01:00) compares equal to its UTC instant, but hashes like the first pass (PEP 495 leaves `fold` out of the hash).
A column mixing both time zones therefore does not match such a belief to itself. Depending on the size of the frames, this shows up in one of two ways:

- **Crash:** the save fails with `Categorical categories must be unique`.
- **Silent:** unchanged beliefs in the repeated hour are kept and saved again as new beliefs.

We found this while a simulation saved a few weeks of quarter-hourly beliefs in local time across the October clock change.

- [x] `_belief_keys_per_row` converts event starts and belief times to UTC, so keys from frames in different time zones line up.
- [x] Added a test with two days of quarter-hours over the clock change: stored in UTC, candidates in Europe/Amsterdam, one changed value in the repeated hour. Before the fix, it fails, keeping three unchanged beliefs besides the changed one. After the fix, it passes.
- [x] Added a changelog entry.

## How to test

```
pytest flexmeasures/data/tests/test_time_series_services.py
```

## Further improvements

timely-beliefs may have similar spots where frames in different time zones are combined into one column. Worth a look as a follow-up there.

## Related Items

Found during aFRR simulation runs over the clock change.

prs.author: gearnode
prs.title: Read the Linux password length PAM enforces
prs.body:
The Linux password policy check read only `PASS_MIN_LEN` from `/etc/login.defs` and passed for any non-negative value. On Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, and RHEL, PAM decides the length, so a host with no real policy (`PASS_MIN_LEN 0`) passed and a host whose policy lives in `pwquality.conf` failed when `login.defs` omitted the setting. The check now reads the length that password changes actually use: - The check counts a `pam_pwquality.so` or `pam_cracklib.so` line in `/etc/pam.d/common-password`, `system-auth`, or `password-auth` only when its control rejects a failure: `required`, `requisite`, or a bracket whose `authtok_err` or `default` action is `bad` or `die`. Unset bracket values default to `bad`, as in libpam. `optional`, `sufficient`, and ignoring brackets enforce nothing. - `password include`, `password substack`, and `@include` are followed, and the included file is read from `/etc/pam.d` by its basename. A missing target or a cycle is unknown. - For pwquality, the length is read in libpwquality's order: `pwquality.conf.d/*.conf` in name order, then `pwquality.conf`, which wins. A `minlen=` module argument overrides both. Values below 6 are raised to 6, as libpwquality does. - When `minlen` is unset, the module default applies: 8 for `pam_pwquality`, 9 for `pam_cracklib`. If several enforcing modules are present, the strictest one is used. - `PASS_MIN_LEN` applies only to a stack that loads no enforcing quality module. - PAM lines drop everything after `#` and join backslash-continued lines. When more than one of those stacks exists, the weakest length is the result. A minimum below 8 fails. A length that cannot be read is unknown. Evidence records the source (`pwquality.conf`, `pwquality.conf.d`, `pam`, `pam_pwquality`, `pam_cracklib`, `login.defs`, or `none`) and still reports `pass_min_len_value`, so the console keeps showing the observed length. The check does not evaluate PAM jumps such as `[success=2]` on earlier lines that could skip a quality module. Reported in https://github.com/getprobo/probo/issues/2350.
  
--- ## Summary by cubic Fixes the Linux password policy check so it reads the minimum length PAM enforces at password changes rather than only `PASS_MIN_LEN` from `/etc/login.defs`. The check reads `minlen` from `pwquality.conf` and its drop-ins, `minlen=` arguments on `pam_pwquality`/`pam_cracklib` lines, and module defaults, following PAM `include`, `substack`, and `@include` lines. It falls back to `login.defs` only when no enforcing quality module is loaded. A module counts only when its PAM control rejects a failure, pwquality values below its floor of 6 are raised, and when several stacks exist the weakest length is the result. Lengths below 8 fail, and unreadable policies or unresolved includes report as unknown. ### Tests **`+515`** **`-11`** - Covers pwquality.conf and drop-in ordering, PAM arguments, controls, includes, and comments, module defaults, the weakest-stack rule, and the login.defs fallback. ### Coredata **`+2`** **`-1`** - Updates the evidence parser comment for the new source values. ### Service **`+612`** **`-30`** - Adds the password-length reading logic, PAM include and control semantics, and the 8-character pass/fail threshold in `linux_password.go`. ### Other **`+11`** **`-0`** - Records the fix in the probo-agent changelog. Written for commit d1dab96810e940f442c143a7b7fe4cdf0b5f1f9a. Summary will update on new commits.

prs.author: gearnode
prs.title: Fix slow and stalled collaboration document loads
prs.body: Documents intermittently took 25–60 s to open in production, or never opened. Logs showed `document collaboration failed … failed to acquire lock: context canceled`. A browser trace showed the server answering the websocket `join` instantly and then sitting on the document `request` until the load balancer closed the idle socket at 60 s. ## Root cause: quadratic remote text insertion Applying the affected document's 64 changes took **98 s** in our Go Automerge engine and **0.5 s** in the JS reference implementation. To place a remote insertion, the engine walked the parent chain of every row after the anchor (`directSequenceBranchRoot`). In normally typed text that chain is as long as the text. The fix relies on RGA ordering: an anchor's subtree is contiguous right after it, so a row's branch follows from its parent alone, and the walk stops at the first row outside the subtree. On the production data: - Applying the changes now takes **0.63 s**. - Text and all 90 marks are identical to the JS result. ## Design weakness that turned it into a stall Every connection ran its own 500 ms refresh. Each refresh held the room's document lock while it read the snapshot plus the whole change log from Postgres and rebuilt the document. A joining peer's `request` needs that same lock. The room now refreshes once for all its peers: - **Trigger:** a Postgres notification or a 500 ms poll. - **Read:** only the change-log rows after the room's known position, read **outside** the lock. - **Lock:** held only to apply those rows in memory. - **Wake:** peers are woken only when the document actually moved. - **Fallback:** after a compaction drops rows the room never saw, the next refresh rebuilds from the snapshot, still outside the lock. - **Bounds:** each refresh has a 10 s timeout and is retried at the next poll. - **Persist:** its catch-up applies the change log the same way instead of rebuilding. ## Also in this branch - The console aliases `cbor-x` to its no-eval build, so its `new Function('')` probe stops triggering `script-src` CSP reports. ## Testing - **Parity and benchmark:** `TestApplyChanges_RemoteRunIntoLongText` compares the Go and reference engines. `BenchmarkApplyChangesRemoteRunIntoLongText` takes 1.72 s per run without the fix and 0.084 s with it. - **Unit tests:** - `TestRefreshDelta_Apply` covers new changes, keeping local edits, changes already held, a gap in the change log, and the rebuild fallback. - `TestRoom_RefreshesWithoutHoldingDocumentLock` checks that the lock stays free during a refresh's read. - `TestRoom_NotifiesOtherPeers` checks that notifications collapse into one room refresh. - **Suites:** `go test` passes for `./pkg/automerge/...`, `./pkg/collaboration/...`, `./pkg/server/api/collaboration/...` and `./pkg/probo/...`. The e2e `TestDocument*` tests pass. - **Manual, two `probod` instances on one database, one browser tab on each:** - Edits crossed instances in 0.13–0.28 s, including a 38k-character paste and edits deep inside it. - 520 interleaved edits from both instances converged to identical text, and the change log was compacted partway through. - All 22 reloads (before and after compaction) loaded the full document, in about 1.1–1.2 s for the tab in front. Background tabs took longer only because Chrome throttles their timers. - No collaboration errors in the logs. After deploying, reopen the affected document (`UGhjAL4vAAEACgAAAZ8SUNe9rj-D0_qM`) in a few tabs and check that the `failed to acquire lock` errors are gone. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes collaboration documents that took 25–60 s to open in production or never opened, caused by quadratic remote text insertion and a room refresh that held the document lock. Remote insertion now uses RGA ordering to walk an anchor's subtree instead of the parent chain, and each room refreshes once for all its peers, outside the lock. The console stops raising CSP `script-src` violations by aliasing `cbor-x` to its no-eval build. ### App: console **`+7`** **`-0`** Aliases `cbor-x` to its no-eval build so its `new Function('')` probe no longer triggers `script-src` CSP reports. ### Service **`+273`** **`-50`** Uses RGA ordering to place a remote insertion by walking an anchor's subtree, stopping at the first row outside it. Applying a 50k-character production document's 64 changes now takes 0.63 s instead of 98 s. Rooms fetch only the change-log rows after their known position, outside the lock, holding it only to apply them; each refresh is bounded by a 10 s timeout, and persist applies the change log the same way. `PutContent` keeps the change-log offset monotonic by bumping `ChangeRevision` past the replaced rows, so a live room's old offset never lands in the new log. An incomplete refresh (a gap compaction left) reports movement alongside the error: the room resets its position so the next round rebuilds from the snapshot, but still wakes peers whose document merged changes. ### GraphQL API **`+99`** **`-119`** Replaces the per-connection refresh loop with one room refresh on a Postgres notification or 500 ms poll. Peers are woken only when the document actually moved, a refresh never blocks a joining peer's request, and a failed or incomplete refresh resets the room position to rebuild from the snapshot next round. ### Tests **`+603`** **`-19`** Adds a parity test comparing the Go and reference engines on remote text runs plus a benchmark that times only the merge. Covers refresh deltas (new changes, local edits, overlaps, log gaps, rebuild fallback), incomplete-but-moving deltas, refresh running without the document lock, and notifications collapsing into one room refresh. Written for commit 062992661ca19a00e624c37d36c2329221ac207d. Summary will update on new commits.

prs.title: fix(anthropic): keep mid-conversation system reminders in one form across turns
prs.body:
## Summary

Claude Code ends every turn with a mid-conversation `role:"system"` reminder that carries the rolling cache marker. The Anthropic converter decided between native `role:"system"` and a `<system-reminder>` user turn by looking at the **next input item's role**. A `tool_use`-led assistant reply arrives as a role-less `function_call` item. So the same reminder went out native while it was the last message (turn N) and wrapped once the reply followed it (turn N+1). The prefix changed at that reminder, its checkpoint stopped matching, and nearly the whole conversation was re-written on every turn.

This was seen on Bedrock InvokeModel with Opus 5.5 after the datasheet set `supports_mid_conversation_system_messages=true` on 2026-11-16. Cached input fell from about 96% to 65%, cost per call rose about 4x, and the write surge hit the Bedrock quota (429s). The datasheet rows have been reverted to `false`.

Replaces #10161, which was built by amending the already-merged #9967 commit and so carried its title and its changes.

## Changes

- **Placement is decided after conversion.** `enforceMidConversationSystemPlacement` (`core/providers/anthropic/responses.go`) checks each run of native system messages against Anthropic's rule, using the messages actually emitted:
  - it must follow a user message, or an assistant message ending in a server tool result;
  - it must end the list or be followed by an assistant message.
  
  Runs that break the rule are inlined exactly as the old inline branch did (trim join, effort-only override first, `inlineMidConversationSystem`). This one check covers `function_call`, `reasoning`, items dropped as empty, and merged turns. The input lookahead (`midConvPlacementOK`) is removed.
- **Released gateways stay safe while the datasheet stays `false`.** Gateways at core ≤ v1.15.2 / enterprise 2.5.x have the lookahead bug and honour the datasheet flag, so it must stay `false` for these rows. A **temporary** list, `midConvSystemPinnedModels` (`core/providers/anthropic/utils.go`), turns the native form on in code for exact versions on Bedrock, Vertex, Mantle and Azure, ignoring the datasheet `false`:
  - listed: `opus-5`, `opus-5-5`, `sonnet-5-5`, `haiku-5-5`, `fable-5`, `fable-5-1`, `fable-5-2`;
  - exact-version match, so `opus-5-6`, `fable-5-3`, `sonnet-5` and Mythos do not match;
  - unlisted models and Anthropic direct keep datasheet-then-default.
  
  The list is removed, and the rows set to `true`, once no supported gateway predates this fix. Until then a new model is added to the list with a test, never by setting the datasheet to `true`.
- `chat.go` only switches to the shared resolver. Its role lookahead is correct on that path, because assistant `tool_calls` keep `Role: assistant`.

**Trade-off:** for listed models the datasheet, including a local override, can no longer turn the native form off. Turning it off takes a release.

**Upgrade note:** gateways change reminder form once on upgrade, which costs one cache re-write per live session.

prs.title: fix(providers): scope stream idle timeout to pending reads
prs.body:
## Summary

Fix provider stream idle timeouts firing while the consumer processes data between upstream reads. With a 100 ms timeout, reading a chunk and spending 300 ms processing it previously closed the body and made the next read return `ErrStreamIdleTimeout`, even though no upstream read was pending.

The timer now runs only during a read. A genuinely stalled read still times out, and cancellation retains its distinct error classification.

## Changes

- Arm or reset the reusable timer when entering `Read` and disarm it on every exit.
- Check the active read and its deadline before acting on a queued timer callback, so a stale callback cannot close a later read prematurely.
- Serialize timeout closure with cleanup, preserving the shared atomic connection-close claim across timeout, cancellation, and response release.
- Preserve expected close-related panic recovery and propagate unrelated read panics after disarming the timer.
- Extend existing tests with deterministic consumer pauses, a real fasthttp chunked response, stale callbacks, cleanup, and cancellation/timeout overlap. Update timeout tests to exercise a pending read.
- Record the HTTP harness coverage gap: Newman cannot deterministically pause the gateway consumer between upstream reads. Delaying an upstream chunk tests a different condition; a controlled post-hook/backpressure fixture is still needed.

### Request-path cost

Go 1.27.3, linux/amd64, AMD EPYC 7K83; medians of three `-benchmem` runs:

| Benchmark | Before ns/op | After ns/op | Before B/op / allocs/op | After B/op / allocs/op |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Read, no context | 125.1 | 256.1 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| Read, with context | 183.0 | 276.3 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| Create, read, cleanup | 526.5 | 462.7 | 376 / 5 | 224 / 3 |

The additional timer synchronization costs about 93–131 ns per read in this microbenchmark; steady-state reads still allocate nothing. Unary paths are unchanged. State is fixed-size per reader: one lazily created timer, a mutex, deadline, flags, and existing body/context references. There is no growing buffer or cache; cleanup stops the timer and prevents further body access by callbacks, and the reader state becomes collectible when its caller releases it. The lifecycle benchmark measures 224 allocated bytes in total per reader operation, not a per-chunk retained allocation.

prs.title: Save steps under paths without spaces
prs.body:
Step file paths now contain no spaces or characters that need quoting, so they work unquoted in shells, globs, `.gitignore`, git pathspecs and URLs on macOS, Linux and Windows.

**This is a breaking change.** Existing `.intent` folders won't match, and their steps need regenerating.

```text
before: .intent/tests/checkout.spec.ts/checkout - guest buys a shirt/add the blue shirt to the cart.ts
after:  .intent/tests/checkout.spec.ts/checkout--guest-buys-a-shirt/add-the-blue-shirt-to-the-cart.ts
```

## Rules

Each folder and file name:

- is lowercased and normalised to NFC, as before
- keeps only letters and digits from any script, plus `.`, `_` and `-`
- drops apostrophes (`don't` → `dont`)
- turns everything else into `-`, including spaces, `{}`, `[]`, `#`, `%`, `$`, `!`, `&` and quotes, so `sign up as {email}` → `sign-up-as-email`
- collapses runs of `-`, and trims `-`, `.` and `_` from both ends, so names can't look like flags or hidden files
- is cut to 64 characters, and to no more than 150 bytes, to stay under Windows' 260-character path limit
- gets a leading `_` if Windows reserves it, now including names with an extension like `con.backup`

Other changes:

- **Titles join with `--`.** Since `-` runs collapse inside a name, describe `a` with test `b c` no longer collides with a test titled `a - b c`.
- **Test file folders are slugified too.** `my tests/sign up.spec.ts` becomes `my-tests/sign-up.spec.ts`, and `..` becomes `_`.

## Testing

- `pnpm tsc`, `pnpm lint` and `pnpm test` pass, with new unit tests for the rules above.
- `pnpm test:e2e`: all 112 flows pass. The checkout step paths now live in `test-e2e/harness/shop-steps.ts` as literal strings.

prs.author: ostenbom
prs.title: Add a remote step store with shared(), and the cache API it talks to
prs.body:
Adds `remoteStore` from `playwright-intent/remote-store`, so CI runs share generated steps through a cache API instead of committing them, and `@playwright-intent/cache-api`, the H3 library it talks to. Only `shared()` is built: every branch reads and writes `main.zip`.

```ts
const intent = {
	model,
	store: remoteStore({
		url: "https://intent-cache.example.com",
		token: process.env.INTENT_CACHE_TOKEN,
		updates: shared(),
	}),
} satisfies IntentOptions;

export default defineConfig<IntentUseOptions>({
	reporter: [["list"], ["playwright-intent/reporter", intent]],
	use: { intent },
});
```

## How it works

- **Download:** store providers get a `prepare` hook, which the reporter starts as soon as it's created, before global setup and web servers.
  - It downloads `main.zip` into `.intent`, skipping test folders already on disk, so local work wins.
  - Workers find the result through an environment variable that points at a status file. The first step read waits for it.
  - A 404 means no steps yet. Any other failure is an `IntentStoreError` in every test, so an outage can't trigger regeneration.
  - It also runs under `merge-reports` and `--list`, where a failed download changes nothing.
- **Upload:** only runs with `CI` set upload, and forks don't. `deliver` fetches `main.zip`, applies the writes and deletes from passing tests, and PUTs it back. A shard doesn't upload; `merge-reports` uploads for the whole run. The last write wins, with no locks.
- **Cost:** one GET per run, plus a GET and a PUT when a step changed.

## `@playwright-intent/cache-api`

- **Endpoints:** `GET`/`PUT` on `/v1/zips/main` and `/v1/zips/branches/:branch`, built like `trace-api`.
- **Storage:** `createS3Storage`, `createR2Storage` (a Workers binding, with no S3 keys) or `createFileSystemStorage`, plus `resolvePath` for tenants.
- **Auth:** you add your own middleware. The README has a Workers example and lifecycle rules for `branches/`.

## Other changes

- **New dependency:** `fflate`, for the zips.
- **Store interface:** `IntentStoreProvider` gets `prepare?`, and `IntentStoreError` is new.
- **Reporter given no options:** it now also throws when a project's store has `prepare`, not only when the store delivers.
- **Release:** the release script and workflow now publish both packages.

## Testing

- **Local:** `pnpm tsc`, `pnpm test` (50 unit tests), lint and format pass. `pnpm test:e2e` passes 112 flows.
- **New flows:** 12, against the real `cache-api` on a local port. They replace the old directory stand-in. They can also run against a real bucket with the `INTENT_E2E_S3_*` variables, and they passed against a local S3-compatible server.
- **Real infrastructure:** a Worker running `cache-api` with an R2 binding, in the Endform - Dev account, used by `endformdev/intent-test` CI with the real model:

| Scenario | Result |
|---|---|
| First CI run on an empty bucket (intent-test#15) | Got a 404, generated 9 steps, uploaded once |
| Rerun of the same job | Replayed with no model calls and no upload |
| Local run with no model key | Downloaded the steps, replayed in about 2s per test, no upload |
| Two shards plus `merge-reports` (intent-test#16) | The shards didn't upload; the merge job uploaded the one new step |
| App link renamed (intent-test#17) | Repaired in CI, the test passed, and the fix was uploaded |

Overwriting an R2 object resets its `last_modified`, even with identical bytes, so a lifecycle rule on `branches/` only expires branches that stop uploading.

## Not in this PR

- **`isolated()`, `merged()` and `prComment()`.** intent-test#17 showed why `isolated()` matters: under `shared()`, a repair on one branch changes the step for every branch.
- **Pruning `main.zip`.** Folders from reworded or deleted tests stay forever.

prs.title: fix(lite): keep basin deletion tick going past transaction conflicts
prs.body:
## Problem

`tick_basin_deletion` processes a page of pending basins and used `progress.record(result?)`. A transaction conflict on any one basin, for example when `delete_stream` races a concurrent write, returned from the tick. The rest of the page was dropped and waited for the next interval (60s), and the conflict was logged as a failed tick. Stream trim and delete-on-empty already treat a conflict as a blocked item and keep going. (#791)

## Fix

- `BasinDeletionError::is_transaction_conflict`, classified the same way as `StreamDeleteOnEmptyError`: a `Storage` or `DeleteStream(Storage)` conflict, or `DeleteStream(TransactionConflict)`.
- `PageProgress::record_item_result` records a conflict as `Blocked` and otherwise keeps the item's own `ItemProgress`.

The existing `record_result` is not used here because it records every `Ok` as `Completed`. Basin deletion reports `Advanced`, `Completed` or `Blocked` per basin, and counting a blocked cursor reset as progress would bring back the tight rescan loop fixed in #779.

## Test

- `conflicted_item_is_blocked` checks that a conflict counts as blocked, that a blocked page does not continue, that a completed item still does, and that other errors are returned.
- `transaction_conflicts_are_classified` produces a real SlateDB transaction conflict and checks each `BasinDeletionError` shape that carries it, plus a non-conflict error.

Fixes #791. Resolves Detail bug `bug_598473cf`.

prs.author: shikhar
prs.title: fix(common): reject sub-second retention ages and use MIN_STREAM_NAME_LEN
prs.body:
## Problem

**Sub-second retention ages.** `RetentionPolicy::validate` rejected only a zero age. A resource spec (used by `s2 apply` and `s2 lite --init-file`) parses `retention_policy` with `humantime`, so `"500ms"` passed validation. Lite stores basin and stream metadata through the API config type, which holds whole seconds, so it was written as `Age(0)`. Every later read validates the stored value and rejects `Age(0)`, so the basin or stream could no longer be read, reconfigured or deleted through the API. (#747)

**Stream name minimum length.** `StreamNameStr` validation checked `name.is_empty()` instead of `name.len() < caps::MIN_STREAM_NAME_LEN`, unlike basin names. `MIN_STREAM_NAME_LEN` is 1, so behavior is unchanged today.

## Fix

- `RetentionPolicy::validate` also rejects an age that is not a whole number of seconds, with `age must be a whole number of seconds`. That covers every non-zero age under 1s. Values arriving through the API are always whole seconds, so stored metadata is unaffected. The resource-spec schema description says so, and `cli/schema.json` is regenerated.
- Stream name validation compares against `MIN_STREAM_NAME_LEN`, with the same message shape as basin names: `stream name should be at least 1 bytes in length`.

One visible change: `s2 apply` with an age such as `"90s 500ms"` used to truncate it to 90s and now rejects it.

## Test

- `retention_policy_age_valid` / `retention_policy_age_invalid` in `s2-common` cover 0, 500ms and 1.5s (rejected) and 1s and one week (accepted).
- `validate_rejects_sub_second_retention_policy` in `s2-resource-spec` checks that a spec with `"500ms"` or `"1s 500ms"` fails validation.
- `min_len` and `too_short` cases added to the stream name validation tests.

`just test`: 960 passed.

Fixes #747. Resolves Detail bugs `bug_066e47bc` and `bug_0909851f`.

prs.title: fix(sdk): settle terminal producer and session reservations
prs.body:
After a terminal producer or append-session error, a submission can wait indefinitely for capacity held by an unrelated reservation. Later batching validation can also hide an earlier append's outcome.

Settle producer tickets and close byte/count capacity before command draining can wait on outstanding permits. Byte waiters and late reserved submissions receive the sticky terminal cause. Already-ready acknowledgements are delivered before unresolved tickets are failed. Later batching-validation failure closes the internal session and forwards earlier submitted batches' acknowledgements or session errors; unsent records retain the validation error.

Keep `AppendPermits` and the existing command-channel closure order. No public API is added. Use `tokio::task::coop::unconstrained` when preserving ready acknowledgements so cooperative yielding does not hide a ready result.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Terminal failure] --> B[Settle earlier tickets and close capacity]
    B --> C[Wake failed controls and capacity waiters]
    C --> D[Drain late reserved submissions]
```

Application incidence is unknown. Earlier appends still depend on normal session deadlines and reconnect behavior.

The cooperative-budget acknowledgement path has no native regression test.

The two public-API regressions in `sdk/tests/stream_ops.rs` add exactly 52 lines, including attributes and blank separators. They cover producer validation draining and byte waiters, plus append-session byte/count waiters.

prs.author: blakeaowens
prs.title: fix(findings): check each moved finding's engagement on Set as Original
prs.body:
**Description**

Set as Original (`POST /api/v2/findings/{finding}/original/{new_original}/`, the classic Set as Original button, and the Similar Findings menu) moves the page finding's whole cluster under the new original: the page finding, its old root, and the old root's other duplicates. Only the page finding was checked against the engagement deduplication rule. The old root and the other duplicates were re-pointed with no check of their own engagements, so they could land under an original in another engagement while `deduplication_on_engagement` was enabled. The old root also got `duplicate = True` but kept `active = True` (and `verified`), so it stayed open beside its new original. The same happened to the page finding when Set as Original ran from the root's own page.

Reproduced on `dev`: one product, engagement A with `deduplication_on_engagement=True`, engagement B with it off. The old root is in B, the page finding (its duplicate) and an open finding are in A. Setting that open finding as the original answered 204 and left the old root `duplicate=True, active=True` in B, under an original in A.

### What changed

- `set_finding_as_original_with_reason` applies the rule `mark_finding_duplicate` already applies to the members it moves. The old root, and every other duplicate in the cluster, is refused when it sits in another engagement than the new original's and either engagement has `deduplication_on_engagement`. The message names that finding and the finding whose duplicate status to reset first. The duplicates take one grouped query (one row per engagement in the cluster), the same number of queries at any cluster size.
- The old root becomes an inactive duplicate (`active=False`, `verified=False`) like every other member, both from a duplicate's page and from the root's own page.
- The Similar Findings menu (`calculate_possible_related_actions_for_similar_finding`) offers Set as Original only where the route accepts it: both call `set_as_original_crossing`, which reads the cluster's engagements in one grouped query cached on the page finding, so the menu adds no per-row query. A row left with nothing names the finding that would cross.
- Setting the page finding's own root as the original moves nothing, so it is not refused.
- Docs: the Similar Findings pages (Open Source and Pro) say Set as Original checks every finding it moves and leaves the previous original as an inactive duplicate.

**Test results**

- `unittests/test_set_finding_as_original_engagement.py`: fourteen tests. The first nine that post to the real route and reload the rows (their own product, no fixture). On `dev` all nine fail for the reported reasons: the four refusal cases (old root or a duplicate crossing, with the setting on either side) answer 204 and move the finding, and the five move cases leave the old root `active=True, verified=True`. With this change all nine pass. Five more cover setting the current root as the original (nothing moves, not refused) and the menu (a hidden offer, the named finding, the offer where the route accepts it, the cluster read once per page).
- `unittests/test_similar_finding_related_actions.py`: three expectations that asserted the old offer now match the route.
- The neighbouring modules pass with the change: `test_mark_finding_duplicate_self_reference`, `test_manual_duplicate_onto_mitigated`, `test_similar_finding_related_actions`, `test_deduplication_logic`, `test_finding_model`, `test_permissions_audit` and `test_rest_framework` (1206 tests).
- Cost, measured on a cluster of one root and 204 duplicates: the checks add 1 query from the root's page and 2 from a duplicate's page (first request on each: 2518 to 2519, 2524 to 2526, measured again on the final revision). Wall time over three interleaved before/after rounds of five runs each is within run-to-run noise (medians 3.6 to 4.8 s either way); the per-member save loop dominates and is unchanged.
- `ruff check` with ruff 0.16.10 and `ruff.toml`: clean.

**Documentation**

Updated `docs/content/triage_findings/finding_deduplication/OS__similar_findings.md` and `PRO__similar_findings.md`.

prs.author: blakeaowens
prs.title: fix(importers): name a reimport's new finding group from its stored title
prs.body:
**Description**

With `group_by=finding_title`, an import and a reimport named the same title's finding group differently:

- the import groups a finding after it is saved, so it names the group from the stored title, which `Finding.save()` title-cases and truncates (`Finding.persisted_title`): "Findings in: Group Jira Rule 0";
- the reimport groups a new finding before it is saved (`DefaultReImporter.process_finding_that_was_not_matched`), so it named the group from the parsed title: "Findings in: group jira rule 0".

For a report whose titles are not already title-cased, a reimport therefore put its new findings into a second group with the same meaning as the existing one. That second group has no JIRA issue, so with JIRA keep-in-sync the new findings never reached the issue of the group they belong to.

This change gives `get_group_by_group_name` an `unsaved` flag. With it, a `finding_title` group is named from `Finding.persisted_title(title)`, the title the row will carry. `process_finding_groups` passes the flag through, and the reimporter's new-finding path is the only caller that sets it. The import, the other `group_by` options, and `group_findings_by` (which reads saved findings) are unchanged.

Two cases keep their old grouping:

- A test can already hold a group that an earlier reimport named from the raw title ("Findings in: group jira rule 0"), and that group is the one its JIRA issue hangs off. The reimporter records each group's raw-title name where it differs (`legacy_group_names`), and `add_findings_to_auto_groups(..., legacy_names=...)` reads those groups in the same lookup: a name with no group of its own joins the oldest of them instead of starting a title-cased group beside it. No query is added.
- A finding without a title stays ungrouped: only a non-empty title is transformed.

`titlecase()` is not cheap (about 0.3 ms per title on the measuring host), and a reimport grouped by title names many new findings that share each title. So the transform is memoized per distinct title (`functools.lru_cache(maxsize=4096)` on a module-level helper).

**Measurements** (Postgres-backed stack on a shared, loaded host)

- Reimport of 2,000 new findings over 50 lower-case titles into a test imported with one finding per title (`POST /api/v2/reimport-scan/`, 3 runs each):

  | | groups after reimport | queries | wall time, median (range) |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | before | 100 (50 split off) | 165 | 10.32 s (9.96 to 11.72) |
  | after | 50 | 162 | 11.64 s (10.44 to 11.66) |

  The wall-time difference is within the host's run-to-run noise (load average around 30; the same code varied by 3.6 s between runs). The naming cost itself, isolated:
- Naming 10,000 new findings (`get_group_by_group_name`, `finding_title`): 50 distinct titles, 3.03 s with an unmemoized `persisted_title`, 0.18 s memoized (the old raw-title name took 2 to 5 ms). With 10,000 distinct titles the memo cannot help and the cost is one `titlecase()` per new finding (3.09 s), the same transform `save()` already applies to each of them.

**Test results**

- `unittests/test_reimport_group_by_title_case.py` (new): imports a Generic Findings Import report with lower-case titles under `group_by=finding_title`, attaches a JIRA issue to each group as an earlier push would, then reimports the report with one new finding per title. It asserts one group per title holding the imported finding and the new one, and that JIRA keep-in-sync pushes each of those groups (`push_to_jira` mocked). On `dev` it fails with the two extra groups (`Findings in: group jira rule 0` and `... 1`, each holding only the new finding); with this change it passes.
- `test_reimport_new_findings_join_a_group_an_earlier_reimport_named_from_the_raw_title` (new): an import without grouping, then a group named from each raw title with a JIRA issue (the state an earlier reimport left), then a reimport with one new finding per title. Without the raw-title lookup it fails with a second, title-cased group per title; with it, the raw-title group holds both findings and keep-in-sync pushes it.
- `test_unsaved_finding_without_a_title_has_no_title_group` (new): a `None` or empty title names the same (no) group saved or unsaved. Without the non-empty guard it fails with `None != ''`.
- `unittests/test_reimport_finding_group_duplicates.py` built its expected group name from the parsed title (its comment said so: the name the reimport used to give the group). It now uses `Finding.persisted_title`, the name an import gives the same group. Unedited, it fails with this fix (4 failures, 1 error, the same set CI reported); updated, its 5 tests pass.
- `unittests/test_importers_auto_finding_groups.py`, `unittests/test_reimport_finding_group_jira_queries.py`, `unittests/test_reimport_finding_group_duplicates.py` and the new tests: 20 tests pass.
- `ruff check` (pinned 0.16.10) passes on the whole tree. `ruff format` is not run by this repo's workflows and is not applied here (1,570 files on `dev`, including the importer files this change edits, would be reformatted by it).

**Documentation**

A bug fix with no new setting, option or screen: no documentation change.

prs.title: feat(gcs): keep MD5 in listings so metadata changes are not content changes
prs.body:
**We are changing `File`: it gets two new fields, `md5` (this PR) and `is_deleted` (#2052).** One schema change, the two PRs merge together. Datasets and listings saved before read as before, with `md5=""` and `is_deleted=False`.

On GCS the `etag` changes on any metadata update (ACL, storage class), so `delta` reprocessed unchanged files, `file_diff` reported them as modified, and reads without versions failed with "changed on the source". GCS listings return each object's MD5 for free; agents bypassed DataChain to get it.

`File.md5` is filled on GCS, empty elsewhere. Where both rows have it, `file_diff`, read checks and the cache key use it instead of `etag`. `read_storage(delta=True)` on GCS keys on `(path, version)`: a generation changes with the content, not with metadata. S3, Azure and other storages are unchanged.

prs.title: perf(parquet): read only the columns a chain uses
prs.body:
`read_parquet` loaded every column into the warehouse, even when the chain used two of them. Before the chain runs, the read now gets only the columns that later steps need: those in `select`, `group_by`, `count` and `gen`, plus the columns used by `filter`, `order_by` and `mutate`. If a step's columns can't be known (`map`, joins, raw SQL), every column is read. This is the column part of #2022.

|---|---|---|
| `read_parquet(...).select(...)` | 137 s, 1.7 GB | 12 s, 0.2 GB |
| `read_parquet(...).filter(...).select(...)` | 279 s, 1.3 GB | 12 s, 0.2 GB |

A row stays when a later list omits it, and deleting the connector account only clears the link. --- ## Summary by cubic Adds asset inventory for AWS accounts: each external account becomes an asset source, a worker lists CloudFront distributions from us-east-1, and discovered rows are stored in a new `assets` table with an `InventoryAsset` type. prs.author: webmixgamer
prs.title: fix(asks): a credential ask is never recorded for a reader who cannot fill it - queue file and blocked clients (#4599)
prs.body:
## Summary

A `credential` ask ends at one door, the Workspace secret field. #4579 made the native raise pick a reader that door opens for (the primary person, else the owner, else a named refusal). Its reviews, in the v1.0.5 release testing, found two more ways to record a reader who cannot fill the ask, and messages that named the wrong cause. This closes them.

- **Queue file.** A `type: "credential"` entry in `~/.trinity/operator-queue.json` is addressed by the same chain as `raise_ask`. The platform picks the reader and ignores the address the agent wrote. An entry that cannot be filed is held and named in the file, and no row is created.
- **Blocked or deactivated people.** A blocked email is never the reader of a credential ask. For approver asks, canon-role asks and gated-skill approvers, a deactivated account cannot open the agent, and the client block stops an email with no account and an account that can only use the Workspace.
- **Messages.** Each refusal names its real cause and a remedy that works, under the same code.

## Changes

**Queue file** (`operator_queue_service/ingest.py`, `filechannel.py`, `ask_service.file_credential_*`)
- The reader comes from `role_addressing.resolve_credential_reader`, read once per agent per sync cycle. Before, the agent's own pick was accepted only when it was the primary on the shared roster, so an owner was never accepted and an entry with no address became a row nobody could fill.
- The entry runs the kind's own raise checks: the name, no options, the destination (stored in its validated form), the context size.
- A held entry stays `pending` in the file and its id is listed in `platform.ingestion` under `role_cannot_open_agent`, `no_person` or `invalid_credential`. A lookup that fails holds the entry for the cycle with no marker and leaves an existing marker as it is.
- The sync fingerprint no longer compares the addressee or the stored destination of a credential row. Both are written by the platform, and comparing them turned the row `changed` one cycle after ingest, which the secret field refuses.
- At most ten destination checks run per cycle.

**Reach rules** (`role_addressing.py`)
- `workspace_reach` / `on_workspace_roster`: a blocked email is not a reader.
- `agent_reach` / `can_open_agent`: a deactivated account cannot open the agent. The client block applies to an email with no account and to a Workspace-only account. A blocked operator or admin can still decide in Operations and stays reachable.
- Both answer yes, no or "could not check"; the yes/no forms fail closed. Each person is read once.

**Refusals** (code `role_cannot_open_agent` is unchanged)
- Credential raise: nobody is seated as primary (assign one), the owner is the primary person (check the owner's access), a system agent (set the credential on the agent), or the platform could not check (try again). A primary who could not be checked is refused, not handed to the owner.
- Approver and canon-role asks: "could not check, try again" when the lookup failed.
- Skill gate: that case answers `503 gate_unavailable`, which a room delivers again, instead of the standing `422 approver_cannot_open_agent`.
- A "cannot open" remedy no longer says "share the agent". A blocked or deactivated person may already have the share, so it says to make sure the agent is shared with them and that they can sign in, and never which one fails.
- An admin's re-address by rule (`409 rule_refused`) is worded from the cause. `409 audience_unchanged` no longer offers the admin seat to a card addressed by role.

**Text**: the `ask_for_credential` tool description says who is asked; the agent prompt names the three hold reasons.

**Docs**: requirements, feature flows, architecture catalogs and user docs. The security report of #4579 gains an addendum for the admin re-address arm. This change has its own report, `docs/security-reports/cso-diff-2026-11-17-4599-credential-reader-doors.md`, with an addendum listing what changed after the audit ran.

No migration. No frontend change.

## Test plan

- [x] `cd tests && pytest unit/test_4599_credential_reader_doors.py -q`: 66 tests, written failing first. One per acceptance line, one per extra fix, each with its control.
- [x] 44 call-site mutations, each restored from a copy: every one turns a named test red.
- [x] The suites of the touched code (asks, role addressing, the credential kind, the file channel, the skill gate, the client block): green, except `test_3785_operator_queue_package.py::test_each_consumer_imported_first_on_a_fresh_install_can_raise_an_alert`, which fails the same way at the base on the machine used (a missing local module).
- [x] `src/mcp-server`: `node --import tsx --test src/operator_queue.test.ts`, 117 of 117. The `ask_for_credential` description is 1,965 of 2,048 characters.
- [x] Full unit suite once, before the merge with `dev`: 41,274 passed. The failures are in 25 files outside this change and fail the same way at the base on that machine.

**Checked by hand on a local instance** (commit `12ad841b2`, before the reworded remedies):
1. A file entry with no address is filed for the owner: `channel: file`, `confirmed`, still `confirmed` 25 s later, and the owner's Inbox shows the masked field.
2. An entry with a reserved name is held: `platform.ingestion` reads `invalid_credential` with the id, and no row exists.
3. A blocked primary with a share is skipped and the ask goes to the owner.
4. A blocked approver with a share is refused `422 role_cannot_open_agent`.
5. Re-addressing a role-addressed credential card answers `409 audience_unchanged`, ending "End it with a reason instead."

**Not run by hand**: the system-agent sentence. It is proven by `TestRaiseWording::test_a_system_agent_is_told_sharing_cannot_help` and `TestAdminReaddressWording::test_a_system_agent_is_told_only_to_end_the_card`. Their limit: they set the system-agent flag on a test agent, so they prove the sentence and the branch, not the flag read on a real system agent.

## Stated limits

- **A card from the queue file carries no role.** It is addressed once, at ingest. It does not follow a later seat change, and an admin's re-address answers `422 unknown_family`; it can only be ended. Pinned by `TestQueueFile::test_a_file_card_has_no_rule_to_be_re_addressed_by`. True of every file row.
- **Point in time.** A later block, unshare or deactivation leaves a pending ask with a reader who can no longer fill it. No writer re-addresses, and the block writer is one more writer without a hook. Ways out today: a primary seat write, an admin's re-address by rule, or ending the ask.
- **A share made after the raise** does not add a seated approver to a pending approver ask. The recorded approver can still answer.
- **Act-as.** "Credentials stay out of act-as" is enforced in the MCP tool only. The REST route accepts an admin's user key acting for an agent for a credential ask.
- **#4189.** Its "done when" refuses the secret field unless the caller is the agent's single primary at answer time. Since #4579 the owner can be the rightful reader while someone else is seated, so that check must be the reader chain.
- **An owner signed in through an outside-client session** gets 404 on their own agent's field: owned agents unlock only for a platform session.
- **An owner lookup that fails** still reads as "the owner has no email", so that outage is not named.
- **The native route's read of the agent's own key** for a `key_env` destination is not run for a file entry. Delivery checks it.
- **Credential rows the file left unaddressed before this change** stay as they are. End them.
- **The destination-check bound.** An entry past ten per cycle waits, unnamed, until the named ones are fixed.
- **Every caller of `can_open_agent`** inherits the block and deactivation checks.

Fixes #4599

prs.author: webmixgamer
prs.title: feat(workspace): answering an ask in the Inbox crosses it off and opens the next one
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Answer, then next.** In the Workspace Inbox, once the server confirms the reader's own answer, the row holds its ended badge for a 150 ms beat, the next pending ask opens (`?item=` by replace, never a push) while the row collapses over 200 ms, and the row then leaves the tab visit. With `prefers-reduced-motion` it happens in one pass. Before this, an answered ask stayed in the list as an ended row and the pane kept showing it, so the reader clicked the next row by hand after every answer.
- **This is the one exception to "rows keep their place" (principle 5).** That rule protects the reader from changes they did not cause, and it still holds for those: an ask ended by another person, by an expiry, by a withdrawal, by the reader in another tab, by a Dismiss, or a failed answer, keeps its row and its selection.
- **#4502.** The "Sent" line said "<agent> is picking this up." for an agent that was not running. The answer response cannot say the wake was deferred, so the card now re-reads the roster and makes that claim only from a roster it just read, for an agent that is not stopped or missing.

## How it works

- The ask card tells the Inbox through a function prop (`notifyAnswered`), on the answer's success path only. Not an emit: the pane is keyed by the item, so a reader who selects another row mid-request unmounts the card, and an emit from an unmounted card is dropped.
- Next = the first pending ask below in the order on screen (so `?sort=` and `?from=` are respected), else the nearest above. Ended rows are skipped, and so are chats.
- **All tab** (the issue asked for this to be decided and noted): an answered ask is still a member of All for 7 days, so its row stays where it is and only the selection moves to the next pending ask. With none left, the selection stays.
- After the last ask the pane says "All caught up" with a next action ("Open Operations" for a platform session, "See what came back" for a Workspace client when Unread has items). A `?from=` filter the reader's own answers emptied is kept, with "Show all agents".
- Stacked layout: no history entry per advance; one Back returns to the list; after the last ask the pane goes back by itself.
- Focus goes to the new ask's heading, and one polite live region says "Answered. Next: <title>." A row that is leaving is inert and never takes focus.
- For 300 ms after an advance opens an ask, its card takes no send (click, Enter, a one-click Approve / Reject), so a late second click cannot answer an ask the reader has not read.
- The collapse is a `grid-template-rows` 1fr → 0fr transition on that one row. No `<TransitionGroup>`: nothing else in the list animates, and a tab change still swaps rows instantly.
- #4502: `refreshRoster()` now resolves `true` only for a read that succeeded. A read that fails, or takes longer than 1.5 s, says "Sent." only, and nothing is drawn while the read is out.

## Changes

- `src/frontend/src/components/portal/PortalInbox.vue`: the sequence, the selection, the caught-up state, the live region
- `PortalInboxList.vue`: the row's two class arms (`done`, `leaving`); the gap between rows moved inside each row so it collapses with it
- `PortalInboxPane.vue`, `PortalAsks.vue`, `PortalCredentialField.vue`: the `notifyAnswered` hook, the guard, the confirmation
- `portalInbox.js`: `nextPendingAsk`, `dropFromVisit`, `answeredAnnouncement`
- `portalUtils.js`, `stores/clientPortal.js`: #4502
- Docs: the requirement (§5.40 and the confirmation rule), `feature-flows/workspace-inbox.md` (a new section naming the exception), `feature-flows/workspace-agents-at-the-centre.md`, `architecture/workspace.md`

No backend change, no migration, no new endpoint or store.

## Stated limits

- The Inbox pane no longer shows a "Sent" line at all (it opens the next ask). The line is now drawn only on a project's "Needs you" card. The tile inside a chat never drew it: it becomes its history row, which is the confirmation there. That is unchanged and now pinned by a test.
- The card's "Agent not yet woken" line leaves with the card on an advance. It is still on the ask in All.
- A second person answering first is a 409 on the card. The row reads pending until the next poll (up to 20 s), then becomes an ended row.
- The tab counter, the sidebar counts and the list head drop when the server confirms, one beat before the row goes.
- Room cards are untouched; a room is never an advance target.
- A reader who answers an agent's last ask under a `?from=` filter and leaves the pane before the server confirms loses the filter.
- The guard covers sends only. Dismiss and Discuss are not held (Dismiss has its Undo).
- A roster whose availability reads `unknown` (the container state could not be read) keeps "is picking this up", as the wake is still attempted.
- Arrow-key stepping between asks is not part of this change.
- jsdom cannot see motion. The specs pin the states and the classes; the collapse itself was checked by eye (below).

prs.title: fix(cli): small fixes to list-streams, bench, update and auth help
prs.body:
Four small, unrelated CLI fixes.

## `list-streams` ignored `--prefix` when the URI had a prefix (#640)

`s2 list-streams s2://basin/a --prefix b` listed streams under `a` and dropped `b`. `s2 ls` already rejected this with "Multiple prefixes provided". The check now lives in `ops::list_streams`, which both commands call, and `ls` no longer repeats it.

## `bench` left its temporary stream behind on failure (#748)

`bench::run(...).await?` returned before the stream was deleted. Now the delete always runs, and the bench error, if any, is returned first. If both fail, the delete error is dropped. The stream still has 1h retention and delete-on-empty as a backstop.

## `update` failed when `s2` was run through a symlink

On macOS `current_exe()` returns the path as invoked. With `s2` symlinked into a directory the user cannot write, such as `/usr/local/bin`, the new binary was staged next to the symlink and the update failed with a permission error. `in_place_update` now canonicalizes the path, as install channel detection in `channel.rs` already does. `self-replace` also canonicalizes before swapping, so the staged file and the swap target are now in the same directory.

## Auth error help assumed an access token (#746)

`UnauthorizedAccessToken` and `MalformedAccessToken` always said to run `s2 auth access-token set` or set `S2_ACCESS_TOKEN`, even when the token came from `s2 login`. The help now uses the recovery step for the token's source, from `recovery_command` in `auth.rs`, which moved to `TokenSource::recovery_command` so both places share it:

| Source | Help |
|---|---|
| browser login | Run `s2 login` again. |
| `S2_ACCESS_TOKEN` | Set S2_ACCESS_TOKEN to a valid access token. |
| stored access token, config file | Run `s2 auth access-token set` to replace it. |

## Test

- `list_streams_prefix_rejects_uri_and_flag_prefix` covers both prefixes (rejected), either one alone, and neither.
- `token_error_help_matches_token_source` checks the help of both errors for each token source, and that browser login help does not mention `access-token set`.
- The bench and update changes have no test. Both paths need a live server or a real release download.

`just test`: 957 passed.

Fixes #640, fixes #746, fixes #748. Resolves Detail bugs `bug_18653bea`, `bug_00fda266`, `bug_7e4dec11` and `bug_6a8c8f39`.

prs.author: dmpetrov
prs.title: perf(udf): read only the input columns a UDF needs, page by key (core data path #2223, phase 5)
prs.body:
Phase 5 of epic #2223. Stacked on #2224 (phase 2, `core-4-listing-fast`), so the diff shows only this step. Independent of the other phase-5 PR; the two merge cleanly together and the merged code passes 4814 targeted tests.


### What
- **Only the columns a UDF reads.** A UDF's input query keeps `sys__id`, the partition id, the columns its params read, and gen's delta keys. An embedding or metadata column the UDF never touches is no longer read, decoded or held in memory.
- **Pages by key, not by OFFSET.** `dataset_select_paginated` continues after the last `(partition_id, sys__id)` it returned. Before, every page re-ran the query and skipped all earlier rows, which made reading the input quadratic in its size.
- **agg seeks its partitions.** The partition table has an index on `partition_id`, and the input joins it, so each page of an agg starts at an index position instead of re-sorting the remaining rows.
- **map streams.** A plain map hands its rows to the writer as one stream instead of a one-row list per row.
- **Shorter batching.** `Batch` and `Partition` use `islice` and `groupby`. The page-size alignment and a duplicate `SELECT_BATCH_SIZE` are deleted.

### Lines
src: 8 files, +95 / −101 (net −6). Tests: +68 / −2.

### Performance
Modal 8 vCPU, 1M rows, seconds, medians; each row measured on one host against phase 2. Saved rows identical.

| operation | phase 2 | this PR | |
|---|---|---|---|
| map | 15.1 | 6.7 | 2.2x |
| agg | 40.9 | 24.8 | 1.65x |
| map over rows with an unused 256-float column | 83.7 | 13.5 | 6.2x, memory 2.8 → 0.9 GB |
| map over File | 41.7 | 28.8 | 1.45x |
| map to a pydantic model | 28.7 | 22.0 | 1.3x |
| gen, read_parquet, tiny operations | — | — | unchanged |

The narrow benchmark rows understate it: real datasets carry columns the UDF does not read, and the old OFFSET paging grows with the square of the row count (agg page reads at 4M rows: 13.7 → 2.1 s on SQLite).

### Tests
- New: keyset paging over ties without OFFSET; `sys__id` required; pruning for map, gen and agg; the partition index.
- SQLite: targeted set (udf, checkpoints, datachain, delta, batching, warehouse, step hashes, signal schema, batch_map, dispatch, pickling) 1670 passed; `score.sh` same.
- ClickHouse (Studio's test setup, local): test_udf, batch_map, checkpoints, warehouse, batching all pass (262 + 193).

### Behaviour
- `dataset_select_paginated` now serves UDF inputs only: it orders by `(partition_id, sys__id)`, ignores the query's own ORDER BY and OFFSET, keeps LIMIT, and raises without `sys__id`. No other caller exists.
- SQLite `create_table` also creates a table's declared indexes; only the partition table declares one.
- Users see no change besides speed.

### Studio
No change needed. Its distributor calls the same pager. For a linear agg on ClickHouse, the partition table should be ordered by `(partition_id, sys__id)`; today it is ordered by `sys__id`, which is correct but scans.

### Review
Antigravity reviewed the prototype; its points applied: the narrowed pager, one map stream (progress counted after `process` succeeds), itertools batching, pruning before the count, the partition index. Rejected: per-partition overhead in `Aggregator.run` (not measurable with 7 groups).

prs.author: joseph-isaacs
prs.title: Read single Delta values from their lane instead of the whole chunk
prs.body:
## Summary

- Depends on spiraldb/fastlanes#226, which adds the single-element undelta used here. `fastlanes` is patched to that PR's commit until it is released, so this PR is a draft until then.

A Delta point read decoded the whole 1024-value chunk holding the row, to return one value. That is expensive wherever something searches or slices sorted Delta-encoded indices.

Compressing StatPopGen with editions disabled showed it. Elements validity compresses to Sparse with Delta-encoded patch indices. Every slice of it binary-searches those indices, and each step of the search decoded a chunk.

Delta transposes each chunk into lanes and encodes every lane against its own base. So a value depends only on its lane's base and its lane's deltas up to its row: 8 to 64 deltas, by integer width. This PR reads just those, through the new `fastlanes` functions.

It is independent of vortex-data/vortex#11452 and #11453 and is based on `develop`.

## Changes

- `delta/probe.rs`: when the deltas are plain or bit-packed on the host, a point read:
  - finds the value's position in the transposed chunk with `fastlanes::untranspose`, and its lane with `fastlanes::delta_lane_row`;
  - reads the lane's base through the bases array;
  - sums the lane's prefix with `undelta_single` for plain deltas, or the safe runtime-width `undelta_pack_single` for bit-packed ones. Both global and per-block widths are supported.
- Patched deltas: the packed sum is corrected for each of the chunk's patches that falls in the lane up to the value's row. The chunk's patches are found by binary search on the patch indices.
- A repeated probe reads one lane on its first visit to a chunk. On a second visit it decodes the chunk and keeps it, as before, so scans within a chunk cost the same.
- Other delta encodings, such as frame of reference, fall back to the chunk decode.
- Tests: every row of a three-chunk array is read through one-off and repeated probes and compared with the decoded array. This covers `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `i32` and `i64`, with plain, globally bit-packed, per-block bit-packed and patched deltas, and with bit-packed bases. The test also asserts these layouts take the lane path.
- `benches/delta_decode.rs`: a `search_sorted` benchmark that runs 64 binary searches over a sorted 256-chunk Delta array.
- `Cargo.toml`: a temporary `[patch.crates-io]` for `fastlanes`. Drop it once #226 is released.

## Performance

`delta_decode` benchmarks, median:

| Benchmark | `develop` | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| `probe_once` (8 one-off reads) | 14.6 µs | 0.58 µs |
| `search_sorted` (64 searches) | 1.20 ms | 0.27 ms |
| `probe_repeated` (8 reads, 2 chunks) | 3.9–6.0 µs | 3.6 µs (within noise) |

StatPopGen's first 10k variants, compressed with editions disabled so Delta is on. These numbers come from an earlier version of this PR that did its own lane arithmetic (median of 3 runs; output byte-identical):

| | `develop` | Earlier version |
|---|---|---|
| Total | 17.2 s | **12.7 s** |
| PID | 3.89 s | 2.26 s |
| PGT | 3.67 s | 1.09 s |

I have not rerun StatPopGen on the `fastlanes`-based version. Its point reads are at least as fast in the benchmarks above.

## Checks run

- `cargo nextest run -p vortex-fastlanes --release`: 1032 passed.
- `cargo clippy -p vortex-fastlanes --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`.
- `cargo +nightly-2026-09-10 fmt`.

Not run: `typos`, which is not installed here.

prs.title: fix(mysql,mariadb,tidb,oceanbase): record the database a cross-database foreign key references
prs.body:
The MySQL-family syncs never read which database a foreign key references, so `ForeignKeyMetadata.ReferencedSchema` stayed empty and a key from `db2.child` into `db1.parent` looked like a key into `db2.parent`. Prior backup needs the real target to refuse a DELETE or UPDATE of `db1.parent` that cascades into `db2.child` (the omni change follows in bytebase/omni#1158 and a pin bump after it).

## Change

- **MySQL and MariaDB** (`db/mysql`), **OceanBase** and **TiDB** read `KEY_COLUMN_USAGE.REFERENCED_TABLE_SCHEMA` and fill `ReferencedSchema` only when it differs from the key's own database. A same-database key, qualified or not, stays empty, so nothing that already works changes.
- **TiDB** gets the column from `KEY_COLUMN_USAGE` because its `REFERENTIAL_CONSTRAINTS.UNIQUE_CONSTRAINT_SCHEMA` names the key's own database even for a cross-database key (seen on v8.5.0). Using `KEY_COLUMN_USAGE` everywhere keeps the four syncs alike. Both queries still filter on the synced database, so MariaDB's pruning (Error 1969 on large instances) is unaffected.
- **SQL Editor column panel** (`ColumnsTable.tsx`): a single-schema engine's key into another database is labeled `db2.parent(id)` from the key itself. It used to look the table up in this database's metadata, which does not hold it, and would render `()`.

## Consumers of `ReferencedSchema` (checked for same-database keys: no change)

| Consumer | Same-database key | Cross-database key |
|---|---|---|
| omni `mysql/catalog` DDL (`definition.go`, `metadata_load.go`) | empty → unqualified, as before | qualified `` `db2`.`parent` `` (was a wrong local reference) |
| omni `tidb`/`oceanbase` `catalog/metadata_load.go` | empty, as before | `TableRef{Schema: "db2"}` |
| omni `{mysql,mariadb,oceanbase}/review` | empty or own name → local, as before | another database |
| `schema/differ.go` `foreignKeysEqual` | empty on both sides | differs once from a snapshot taken before this change, then stable |
| `aireview/catalog_definition.go` | unqualified, as before | qualified |
| frontend schema diagram, schema editor sheet, `ForeignKeysTable` | empty → current schema, as before | diagram skips the edge (no such schema); table shows `db2.parent.id` |

## Evidence

`TestSyncForeignKeyReferencedDatabase` creates a table with three keys — unqualified, qualified with its own database, and into another database with `ON DELETE CASCADE` — and requires only the third to name the database:

- MySQL 8.0.33 and MariaDB 11.8.8 (`db/mysql`), TiDB v8.5.0 (`db/tidb`): shared testcontainers, run in CI.
- OceanBase 4.3.5.6 (`db/oceanbase`): gated on `OCEANBASE_WALK_DSN` like the package's other sync tests; run locally on `oceanbase/oceanbase-ce:4.3.5.6`.

Making the condition always fill the field, or never, fails all four.

prs.author: Aditya-thesys
prs.title: feat(react-ui): a reopened dashboard is on the filters the user left it on
prs.body:
Stacked on #1607; the diff here is only this change.

## What

A reopened dashboard starts on the filters (its `$state`) the user left it on, instead of the defaults, and shows its last results for those filters while the data reloads.

## How

All in `useLastResults.ts`, on top of the last-results feature:

- **Save.** The state the `Renderer` reports through `onStateUpdate` is saved as one more entry beside the query results (key `$state`, value `{ version, state }`), half a second after the last change and when the content closes with a change pending. Nothing else is stored, and the entry is exactly what `onStateUpdate` reported.
- **Restore.** The one read of saved entries now starts when the dashboard's content is shown. If it holds a state for the version on screen, that state is given to the `Renderer` as `initialState` before its queries first run, so they run once, with the restored values. An app's own `initialState` wins key by key, and its `onStateUpdate` is still called.
- **Hold.** The program is held back until that read settles, at most 400 ms, so the queries do not run twice. After the bound the defaults are used and a state that arrives late is never applied (it would overwrite what the user has chosen since).
- **Results of later queries are saved too.** A query that runs after the first batch (a filter refetch, a refresh) is saved under its own key. Nothing more is answered from saved results than before; this only means the restored filters have results to show on the next open.

Off together with the last results: a storage without the two methods, or `cacheQueryResults: false`, has no read, no hold and no save. No changes in `lang-core` or `react-lang`.

## Checked in a browser

On the assistant-ui dashboards example, a dashboard with a "Time Range" filter (default 6 months), the data route slowed by 2 seconds, the page sampled on every animation frame:

| | On reopen |
|---|---|
| Changed to 3 months, reloaded, reopened | "Last 3 Months" and the saved 3-month figures from the first frame the dashboard appeared (230 ms); fresh figures at 2.2 s |

- No frame showed the default filter or zeros.
- The dashboard appeared no later than without this change: the saved entries arrived before the dashboard was ready, so the hold did not delay it.

## Known limits

- When the read of saved entries is slower than loading the dashboard itself, the dashboard appears up to 400 ms later.
- `isLoading` is also true during that hold.
- Every filter combination a user tries becomes a saved entry, within the storage's own limits.

## Tests

Through the real `Renderer`: a filter change saves the state once, debounced; a reopen starts on the saved filter, makes one call per query with its arguments and shows the saved result for them; a state saved for another version restores nothing; an app `initialState` wins; a storage without the methods has no hold and uses the defaults; a slow read gives the defaults after the bound and the late state is not applied; a query after the first batch is saved under its own key. One last-results test now waits out the 400 ms bound, and one now expects the later query's entry to be saved.

prs.title: Record durable student usage of copied questions
prs.body:
# Description

This builds on the course and institution adoption counts in #16371 and lays the groundwork for future Content Hub impact metrics. The goal is to help question authors understand how many students actually used their questions, rather than counting everyone enrolled in a course containing a copy.

Matt proposed a dedicated usage table containing the source question, destination course, course instance, assessment, and student. This PR follows that proposal: it records usage when an answer is saved and uses a unique key to prevent duplicate records for repeated submissions in the same context. The identifiers intentionally have no foreign keys, allowing usage history to survive deletion of the original records.

Nathan raised concerns about the cost of counting students through the existing activity tables, so we benchmarked that query in production and compared a usage-table prototype locally before choosing the approach. In synthetic tests, the prototype reduced a 100-question report from about **34 ms to 1.8 ms**, while adding roughly **0.2–0.7 ms** per simplified submission transaction. These are local measurements, not production latency estimates.

The table therefore serves two purposes: reducing the work needed for future reports and preserving historical reach. This PR adds recording only. Historical backfill and student-count reporting will follow after recording is fully deployed.

- [x] I have disclosed the level of AI assistance used: the majority of the implementation and tests were written with Codex.

# Testing
