prs.title: fix(core): show missing-export and unresolved-import build errors
prs.body:
Fixes #588

## Summary

`catalyst build` didn't recognise Rollup's `MISSING_EXPORT` error, so the build output showed only stack frames instead of the cause. This PR extracts that error and shows it with its file, line and a code frame. Following review, recognised import errors also get their own catalog codes: `BUNDLE-001` for a missing export and `BUNDLE-002` for an unresolved import. Anything else stays `BUNDLE-000`.

```
reportBundleFailures (src/scripts/build.js)
└─ extractBuildErrors(output, { toolchain: "vite" })   (src/cli/buildErrors.js)
   ├─ match    → bundleCodeFor(message) → BUNDLE-001 | BUNDLE-002 | BUNDLE-000
   │             diagnostic(): code, message, location, code frame, hint, docs
   └─ no match → BUNDLE-000 + fencedTail(): last 8 output lines
```

## Root cause

`VITE_ERROR_PATTERNS` matched only some unresolved-import forms and esbuild transform errors:
- Rollup's `<file> (L:C): "X" is not exported by "Y"` matched nothing.
- Neither did Rollup's plain `Could not resolve "x" from "file"`.
- `Failed to resolve import` used `[^.]*`, which stopped at the first `.` in a path such as `src/App.js`, so it never matched either.

With no match, the report fell back to `fencedTail`, which prints the last 8 output lines. For these errors, those lines are all stack frames.

## Repro

1. Use an app on `catalyst-core@1.1.0` that builds cleanly.
2. In any component, import a name `catalyst-core` doesn't export: `import { Link } from "catalyst-core"`. This is common after the 1.0 migration, which stopped re-exporting React Router. An import of a missing file, such as `import x from "./does-not-exist"`, fails the same way.
3. Run `catalyst build`.

## Fix

- `src/cli/buildErrors.js`:
  - Matches Rollup's missing-export line and plain `Could not resolve "x" from "file"` line.
  - Lets `Failed to resolve import/entry` match paths that contain dots.
- `src/errors/registry.js`: adds `BUNDLE-001` (an import names something its module does not export) and `BUNDLE-002` (an import could not be resolved), each with details and a suggested action.
- `src/scripts/build.js`: `bundleCodeFor(message)` picks the code for each extracted cause, and each block shows that code's doc link.
  - When `hintFor` has no hint, the registry's suggested action is shown instead.
  - `Could not load` stays `BUNDLE-000`, because it also covers non-import ENOENT failures inside plugins.
- `errors/BUNDLE/BUNDLE-001.md`, `BUNDLE-002.md` and `errors/index.json`: generated with `generateDocs`.
- `examples/error-catalog/scenarios/bundle.js`: a scenario for each new code.

## Evidence

Command: `catalyst build`, in the repro app.

Missing export, before:

```
error BUNDLE-000  production build
The server bundle failed
│     at Module.error (.../rollup/dist/es/shared/node-entry.js:18234:16)
│     at Module.traceVariable (...)
│     ...
```

The same block was printed again for the client bundle.

Missing export, after:

```
error BUNDLE-001  server + client bundle
"Link" is not exported by "dist/index.jsx"
at src/js/components/Header/Header.js:3:10

>  3 │ import { Link } from "catalyst-core"
     │          ^

hint  Check the module's exports and update the import name, or install a
      dependency version that exports it.
docs  https://github.com/tata1mg/catalyst-core/blob/main/errors/BUNDLE/BUNDLE-001.md
```

Unresolved import, before: `BUNDLE-000` with `The server bundle failed`, followed by Rollup stack frames, printed once for each bundle.

Unresolved import, after:

```
error BUNDLE-002  server + client bundle
Could not resolve "./does-not-exist"
at src/js/components/Header/Header.js

hint  Check the import path and package.json _moduleAliases, or install the
      missing dependency.
docs  https://github.com/tata1mg/catalyst-core/blob/main/errors/BUNDLE/BUNDLE-002.md
```

## Regression test

- [x] Added tests that fail without this fix and pass with it:
  - `packages/catalyst-core/test/cli/buildErrors.test.ts`: extraction, including the negative case `foo (1:2): "x" is fine`.
  - `packages/catalyst-core/test/scripts/build.test.ts`: classification and the build report output.

## Affected error codes

- `BUNDLE-001`: new.
- `BUNDLE-002`: new.
- `BUNDLE-000`: unchanged for unrecognised failures. Recognised missing-export and unresolved-import failures now use the two new codes.

## Merge danger

```text
Door: two-way, new catalog codes and error display only; reverting restores BUNDLE-000 output.
Blast radius: catalyst build output when a Vite bundle fails, and the error catalog docs; successful builds are unaffected.
```

---

prs.author: radubrehar
prs.title: shadcn theme: a dark mode that follows the `dark` className of the page
prs.body:
## Problem

The `shadcn` theme only had light variables. Most of them are shadcn/ui CSS variables (`--background`, `--border`, `--muted`, ...), so the grid already looked dark on a page with the `dark` className. But 14 variables were not set by the theme at all. They came from the default theme, which picks its light or dark values by the **color scheme of the OS**, not by the page:

- **dark page, light OS:** the pinned column border, the filter editors, disabled rows, row details and the grouping toolbar items kept the light colors of the default theme (`#c6c6c6` borders, `#eeeeee` disabled rows, white toolbar items).
- **light page, dark OS:** the same parts were dark. Disabled rows were dark gray on a white grid.

## Fix

The theme now sets those 14 variables itself, and the mode comes from the page:

- **Light** (no `dark` className): they are fixed to the values they had, the light values of the default theme. They are computed from the default theme's variables at build time, so they can't drift.
- **Dark** (`.dark` on the grid, on an ancestor, or between the theme element and the grid): dark values made from the shadcn/ui variables (`--border`, `--input`, `--muted`, `--background`). The whole variable set is declared again there, so it resolves on the element that is in dark mode.
- `infinite-theme-mode--dark` still works and is still not needed, as the blog post says.
- The theme no longer has a `prefers-color-scheme` block.

Files: `theme-shadcn.css.ts`, `vars-shadcn-light.css.ts`, new `vars-shadcn-dark.css.ts`. No change to the variable contract or to other themes.

## What changes for existing users

Compared with every `--infinite-*` variable before and after, on the new test page:

- **Light page, light OS:** 164 variables, 0 changed.
- **Dark page:** 12 changed (the ones listed above, plus `--infinite-theme-mode`).
- **Light page, dark OS:** now the same as with a light OS.
- `--infinite-theme-mode` is `dark` only on a dark page. Before, it was `dark` whenever the OS was in dark mode. Nothing in the library reads it.

One edge case: an app that switches its shadcn/ui variables with a `prefers-color-scheme` media query, without the `dark` className, is now treated as light for these 14 variables. Adding `infinite-theme-mode--dark` (or `dark`) fixes that. shadcn/ui's documented setup uses the className.

Not changed here: the expand/collapse icon, the focus outline and the filter focus border still use the accent color of the default theme (blue) and not `--primary`. That is the same question as for the older themes, so it is left for a separate decision.

## Tests

`examples/src/pages/tests/table/theme/shadcn-dark` (with a `.page.vue` sibling), a light and a dark grid side by side with no `infinite-theme-mode--*` className:

1. follows the `dark` className of the page (fails on `master`);
2. the light mode keeps its colors (passes before and after);
3. does not depend on the color scheme of the OS: every `--infinite-*` variable of both grids is the same with `prefers-color-scheme` light and dark (fails on `master`, 15 variables differ).

All 6 pass in React and Vue. The whole `theme` spec folder was run as well (53 passed, 4 more passed on retry after first-compile timeouts in dev mode).

A docs note that could go on the theming page (not included, to stay out of the docs content that is being migrated): "The `shadcn` theme takes its mode from the `dark` className of shadcn/ui, not from the OS."

## Note

This changes `source/`, so it ships to npm when merged.

prs.author: GoKubar
prs.title: host: an edit applies to the file as it is when the host's copy is signed within its tick (#1559)
prs.body:
Fixes #1559. Lane SOUND-KEYS.

**Status:** draft. The PC test runs are in progress.

## Bug

`apply_changes` used the host's copy of an edited file whenever the file's stat fields matched the ones signed after the host's last write. The host's own signature is always racy (`StatSig::racy`), because it is taken within the file's time tick. A racy signature misses two kinds of write:
- another program's write in that tick, to the same length;
- a write between the host's `write_all_at` and the `sig()` after it.

After either, the next edit was spliced into the stale copy, and the file mixed two versions.

## Fix

- **Compare the bytes while the signature is racy.** `current` now compares the file with the copy as well (`same_content`: read in 64 KB pieces, nothing kept). On a mismatch it reads the file.
- **Keep the signature taken before the read.** `current` returns the signature it took before reading or comparing, and its callers keep that one. Before, the buffers' path and the no-op edit's path signed the file after reading it.
- **Fields alone once typing pauses.** When typing pauses past the tick, the copy gets a signature that is not racy, and from then on the fields alone suffice, as before.

**Cost:** while the user types, each keystroke reads the edited file once. An upper bound, measured with a Python read-and-compare loop on the M5 Pro (best of 50):

| File size | Time |
|---|---|
| 50 KB | 10 µs |
| 1 MB | 73 µs |
| 4 MB | 262 µs |

**Residual, not changed here:** in the compile that writes the file, the engine's reads go through `system::note_known_content`. That uses the host's copy under the signature taken after the write, so within that one compile, a write in the gap is still read as the host's text.

## Tests

`an_edit_applies_to_another_program_s_write_within_the_tick` simulates the same fields under a racy signature with a different copy. VERIFIED on the Mac, debug build: it fails without the comparison (the edit lands on the stale copy) and passes with it. `edits_leave_the_file_as_the_text` passes. `cargo clippy -p flashtex-engine --tests -D warnings` is clean.

prs.title: liblsoda: take the max in vmnorm0() without a libm fmax() call
prs.body:
Part of #1611.

`vmnorm0()` is liblsoda's weighted max-norm, called several times per step from `stoda()`, `correction()`, `lsoda()` and `orderswitch()`. It called libm's `fmax()` for every state; at R's `-O2` GCC leaves that as a library call. In a callgrind profile of a FOCEi fit (2-compartment oral, 100 subjects, sensitivities, liblsoda) `vmnorm0()` plus `fmax()` were 11% of all instructions (515 million `fmax()` calls in 10 outer iterations).

It now keeps the larger value with a compare. A NaN element leaves the running maximum as it is, as `fmax(vm, x)` does, and the weights are positive, so every result is the same bit for bit.

Measured on a shared 32-core Linux machine, one thread, interleaved with main 761879664 (load average 30-38 from other jobs):

| | main | branch | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| FOCEi full fit, median of 6 | 55.21 s (49.10-57.67) | 48.35 s (46.61-51.34) | -12% |
| FOCEi, 10 outer iterations, median of 8 | 8.235 s (6.461-8.822) | 7.011 s (5.102-7.628) | -15% |
| rxSolve, 5000 subjects x 15 records, median of 15 | 0.969 s (0.752-1.001) | 0.898 s (0.652-0.928) | -7% |

Callgrind, 1000-subject simulation: `par_solve` 1277.5 M -> 1206.5 M instructions (-5.6%).

Bit-identity was verified on Linux by comparing fingerprints (of the `%a` representations) of the FOCEi fit's objective, thetas, omega and etas and of the 5000-subject simulation's states against main. prs.title: import_arrow: refuse text that is not valid in the database encoding
prs.body:
Fixes #2045.

## What was wrong

`pgcolumnar.import_arrow` passed each Arrow UTF8 value straight to the column type's input function. textin, varcharin, json_in and jsonb_in do not check the encoding, because core checks client text before they run, and a file the backend reads skips that step. So a stream holding `ok`, the bytes `ff fe` and a lone `c3` imported 3 rows into a `text` column, and `upper()` and `ORDER BY` on it then failed with `invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8"`. `read_parquet` already refuses the same bytes (`pq_text_cell_ok`).

## The fix

`imp_scalar_at` now checks every UTF8 value with `pg_encoding_verifymbstr(GetDatabaseEncoding(), ...)` before any input function sees it, in a new `imp_text_check`. It mirrors `pq_text_cell_ok`: an all-ASCII value skips the verifier, and a bad one raises 22021 with the same message shape, naming the Arrow column and the first bad bytes. A NUL byte is refused too, as in the Parquet reader. The check sits in one place, above both text branches. Each import node now carries its target column's name, so an element of a `text[]` is named the same way.

**One change from the brief, said plainly:** the brief expected json and jsonb to validate already. They do not. On main, invalid bytes inside a JSON string imported 3 rows into `json` and into `jsonb` (red output below). The check runs before every input function, so json and jsonb now refuse such values too. `bytea` is unchanged and still keeps the raw bytes.

## Red: the new tests on main's code (PG18)


Stacked on #790 (`feat/hardware-sequencer-z-first`). Host **and firmware**: the sequencer wire version goes from 2 to 3.

## What

`SEQ_RUN` now selects a channel of the committed program. Byte 6 of the command: 0 runs every channel (today's run, and what a zero-filled command means), n runs channel n minus 1 alone.

#790 made a Z FIRST acquisition one single-channel burst per channel, and had to re-upload a one-channel program before every burst, because the controller holds one program: 16 acked `SEQ_WRITE` words plus `SEQ_COMMIT` per channel per FOV. With the selector the program is uploaded once per acquisition for both orders, and each Z FIRST burst selects its channel of it.

## Compatibility

The program layout is unchanged, but `kWireVersion` / `WIRE_VERSION` are now 3, so firmware without the selector refuses the new host's programs at commit (`BadProgram`, detail version) and the acquisition fails at preparation with a clear reason, instead of running every channel and failing three bursts later. New host plus old firmware and old host plus new firmware both fail that way. The pairing rule, host and firmware from the same tree, is unchanged. The reported firmware version number is untouched.

## Firmware

- `SeqEngine::start()` takes the channel (`kAllChannels` by default). Step count, the step-to-layer mapping (one step per layer; the channel's z offset applies), the range check and the reported channel count follow the selection. A selector past the last channel fails `BadChannel` with the index as detail before anything moves, next to the `BadDuration` and `StackOutOfRange` refusals.
- `seq_start(stack_start, channel)`; `callback_seq_run()` decodes byte 6; the self-test runs every channel.
- Native tests: a selected channel runs alone (its three planes with its offset, its exposure, then the return to start); a selector past the last channel fails before any DAC write; the golden program bytes and CRC are re-pinned at v3 (`0xEB4E`) in the firmware test and the host mirror.

## Host

- `Microcontroller.seq_run(stack_start, channel=None)`.
- `SequencerProgram.n_frames_for()`, `step_to_layer_channel()` and `check_stack_range()` take the channel; `SimulatedSequencer` runs the selected channel alone and refuses a bad index like the engine.
- Worker: one upload per acquisition; a Z FIRST burst of one channel of a multi-channel program selects it; `_ensure_uploaded` and `build_bursts` from #790 are gone; the burst timeout is sized for the selected channel.
- `tools/sequencer_transport_check.py`: two bench checks between the existing run checks, "run channel 1 alone: Done, 3 frames fired" and "a channel past the program is refused before anything moves (BAD_CHANNEL)".

## Tests

Native: 293 passed. Teensy build (`teensy41_newctrl`): success. Host: the sequencer program, simulator, controller and firmware-sim files, the worker-level Z FIRST file, the end-to-end file and the worker files, all green; collect-only clean; the simulation GUI driver boots and runs the microcontroller and stage.

Bench: the transport check's two new checks, then the Z FIRST sample run of #790 without the per-burst uploads. Flashing is Hongquan's call.

prs.author: bitemyapp
prs.title: Put Panel Self Refresh in the battery menu, off until turned on
prs.body: Panel Self Refresh is now a switch in the battery menu. It shows only where the built-in panel can refresh itself, and it's off until someone turns it on. The display's refresh rate stays whatever Displays sets. The picture is rendered by the shell's panel test (`tests/panels.rs`) at 2x, with fixed battery data. It's not a capture of a live desktop. **Stacked on #232** (`chanoma`). ganymede follows `chanoma` for testing, so this branch builds on it to carry both. I'll retarget it to `main` once #232 lands. ## Why On the ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 14 (Samsung ATNA40HQ10 OLED, Panther Lake, stock xe on Linux 7.3.1), the driver runs the panel with Panel Replay and selective updates: - With Early Transport, which is the driver's default, a line or two flashed across the panel now and then. - With Early Transport off, the flashes stopped, but the display felt laggy at 120 Hz. A blind test confirmed this: over four rounds in a random order (two with Early Transport, two without), the user called both rounds without it laggy and both rounds with it fine. - With panel self refresh off, it was smooth. The kernel version wasn't the cause: 7.3.1 has no drm changes over 7.3.0. Aizome's frame times were fine (0.26 ms median on eDP-1) and the GPU wasn't throttled. What it saves: on the same laptop left idle (Power Saver, 40% brightness, on battery), the platform drew 2.88 W with it off and 1.62 W with it on, about 1.3 W less. That's RAPL psys over eight alternating one-minute rounds; the battery's own meter agrees once it settles. The processor package's share is 0.2 W (0.69 to 0.49 W); the rest is outside it. With it on, the package spent about twice as long in its deepest idle state (PC10), and the display engine powered down (DC5) only then. It saves nothing while the picture keeps changing. ## How - **`aizome_sys::panel_refresh`** reads what the helper found (`/run/aizome/panel-refresh.toml`) and turns the setting on or off through the helper. Its `helper` module does the root side: - It finds the built-in panel's `i915_edp_psr_debug` in debugfs, but only when the driver's status says the panel supports PSR or Panel Replay. - It also reads the driver's `enable_psr` and `enable_panel_replay` options (for the driver bound to the panel's GPU, under `/sys/module`). If they leave nothing the panel can do (0 is never), there's no switch and nothing is written. Linux 7.3 reads them apart, so `enable_psr=0` alone still leaves Panel Replay. - It writes `0` (the driver's default) for on and `1` (no PSR and no Panel Replay) for off. - It keeps the choice in `/var/lib/aizome/panel-refresh`. - **`aizome-panel-refresh on|off|apply`**, a new bin in aizome-sys, installed to `libexec`. It runs through pkexec under its own polkit action `org.aizome.panel-refresh`. That action is `allow_active=yes`, so whoever is at the computer can flip it without a password, as with the power mode. - **The `aizome-panel-refresh` system service** runs `apply` at each start, so the choice survives reboots. It waits up to 10 s for Intel's driver to create its files, and only if an xe or i915 display exists. - **The battery menu** (`systray/panels.rs`, `glue.rs`): - A Panel Self Refresh switch under Keep Awake, with two lines: "The screen keeps its picture by itself while nothing moves: saves battery, can feel laggy." - Turning it shows the new state at once; the helper runs on a thread. - If the helper refuses or fails, the switch goes back to what the status file says. - The `docs/shell.md` battery entry describes it. The switch uses the driver's PSR debug file rather than the `enable_psr`/`enable_panel_replay` module options for two reasons. Writing the file takes effect at once. And `enable_psr=0` doesn't stop Panel Replay in 7.3: it has its own option, and both are read only when the display is next set up. ## Checks On wx at dfa249ac, and the `aizome-sys` checks again at 00c3afc5: - `aizome-sys --lib panel_refresh` (3): - a panel that can is kept off at boot with no choice yet, turned on, and still on at the next `apply`; - no switch, and nothing written, where the panel can't or there's no debugfs; - no switch, and nothing written, where the kernel options leave nothing: Panel Replay still allowed with `enable_psr=0`, none with both at 0, none for a PSR-only panel with `enable_psr=0`. - `aizome-shell --test panels` (9), including the new test: - no switch where the panel can't; - the switch and its lines where it can, at the height the panel's size says; - turning it on shows at once; - a refusal puts it back. - The rest of `aizome-shell`'s tests pass, except `the_whole_screen` and `pictures_of_the_lock_screen`, which fail on wx regardless because they read wallpapers only ganymede has. - `cargo fmt --check` and clippy are clean (except aizome-kit's existing `fetch_update` deprecation). - The package with its check phase, and `aizome-checks.chanoma`, passed (see the comment below). ## Not yet checked - On hardware: installed on ganymede (X1 Carbon Gen 14) at dfa249ac. The boot service ran and found the panel (`available = true`, `on = false`; the debug file reads 1, "PSR mode: disabled"). Turning the switch on from the menu took effect live: the debug file reads 0, "PSR mode: Panel Replay Selective Update enabled (Early Transport)", source status `SU_STANDBY`. Reinstalled at 00c3afc5 with both options at their default (`-1`): the service's `apply` ran again, kept the switch (`available = true`, `on = true`), and Panel Replay stayed on. Not yet seen there: a reboot putting the choice back. - Any panel other than this one, and i915 (as opposed to xe) machines. - The firmware's word: on a built-in panel,

prs.title: Fix silent-failure traps: data patterns, late definitions, inert statements
prs.body:
- **`data` patterns.** A `(data $a $b)` pattern in a `case` branch or clause head is now the tuple
  `($a $b)`, as in a `let` pattern, and its first field is never a functional pattern. Before, it was
  a literal three-element list that never matched what `(data ...)` builds, so the case silently fell
  through. Raw positions (space rows, `match` patterns, `Atom` arguments, quoted payloads) keep the
  literal term, unchanged.
- **Load order.** Call versus data no longer depends on load order. A head that is not yet a
  function records a `late_symbol` dependency, declared or not. A later definition at any arity, or
  an `import_prolog_function`, recompiles the callers. The "defined after already being used"
  warning and the arity-specific `late_call` dependency are removed. A late definition costs a
  second compile of its callers.
- **Underapplied clause bodies.** A function whose body is a partial application compiles with
  the missing arguments in its head. A call at the source arity used to find nothing (an
  existence error, or an empty result after a late recompile); it now returns
  `(partial F Args)`, as any underapplied call does. Lambdas too.
- **Inert statements.** A discarded statement (non-final `progn` or `prog1` element, unused `let`
  binder) that is pure data and whose head is still not a function when the outermost load completes
  is reported: a warning by default, an error under `--strict`. It catches missing or misspelled
  side-effect helpers.
- **`and`/`or` unchanged.** They stay eager, as on main; `and-then`/`or-else` are the
  short-circuit forms.
- **Behaviour changes.** `(f)` for `(= (f) (g 1))` with binary `g` is `(partial f ())` (was an
  error). A caller compiled before its callee is imported now makes the call (`42`, was the data
  `(late_inc 41)` plus a "defined after already being used" warning). A function defined after its
  caller is now called. A `case` over a quoted literal `(data ...)` value no longer matches a `(data $a $b)` pattern; spell the literal head as
  `(data data $a $b)`. **Migration:** search for `case` and clause-head patterns starting with
  `(data` that are meant to match a literal `data`-headed value (from `quote`, a space row or an
  `Atom` argument), and rewrite them as `(data data ...)`. Patterns over constructed values need no
  change.
- **Tests.**
  - New: `data_pattern`, `late_call_recompile` (+ `imports/late_definition/`), `native_arguments`
    (a pin), `strict_inert_statement_late_definition`, `strict_inert_statement_effects`,
    `fail_strict_inert_statement`.
  - Updated: the lifecycle test's dependency name; `curry` gains the source-arity closure cases;
    `test_import_after_use_warns` becomes `test_import_after_use_recompiles_caller` (expects 42).

- **Validation.** `test.sh` exits 0 and `uv run pytest tests` passes (20), as CI runs them; every new test fails on `main` (ee5cacb) and passes here. A downstream project (PeTTaChainer, 163 MeTTa files and ~1,000 Python tests) passes all gates on the patched runtime, and the late-definition fix exposed one real latent bug there (a native call that had always compiled as inert data). Load overhead on ordinary programs measured 0.7–2.0%; a late definition costs a second compile of its callers.
- **Open question for maintainers.** Should the inert-statement check also run for string loads (`process_metta_string`)?
